heuristics.rule: Never choose a PhD program based on a single professor — require at least three faculty members you want to work with
heuristics.condition: When evaluating PhD programs and deciding whether to accept an offer
heuristics.action: Identify at least three faculty members whose research genuinely excites you before committing to a program
heuristics.because: If the one professor you came for leaves, gets tenure denied, loses funding, or turns out to be a poor mentor, you have no fallback — your entire PhD trajectory collapses around a single point of failure

heuristics.rule: Choose a great advisor with mediocre everything else over a great program with a documented red-flag advisor
heuristics.condition: When deciding between School A (strong advisor, weaker resources) and School B (strong resources, advisor with documented issues)
heuristics.action: Prioritize advisor quality; decline the program with documented advisor problems regardless of prestige or resources
heuristics.because: The advisor-student relationship directly determines whether you graduate; lab culture and facilities are secondary — you cannot change a PI's fundamental approach, but you can navigate resource gaps

heuristics.rule: Check whether a professor's publication record consists primarily of co-authorships with their own current or former students
heuristics.condition: When evaluating a potential PhD advisor's publication history during the application or interview stage
heuristics.action: Look up the advisor's recent papers and check co-author affiliations; if nearly all are current or former advisees, ask why they don't publish with peers in the field
heuristics.because: Insularity in publishing signals poor peer collaboration skills, which limits the professional network the advisor can offer you and may indicate other dysfunctional relational patterns

heuristics.rule: Treat current student enthusiasm during campus visits as a signal, not just a formality
heuristics.condition: When attending PhD visit weekends or interviews and speaking with current graduate students
heuristics.action: Listen for hesitation, pauses, and qualified praise ('yeah...it's a really great program') and probe for patterns across multiple students
heuristics.because: Students who genuinely enjoy their program express it naturally; muted or performative enthusiasm after a pause reveals what they cannot say directly

heuristics.rule: Avoid programs that require PhD students to TA 2–3 courses per semester alongside research
heuristics.condition: When evaluating the TA load expectations of a PhD program during interviews or offer review
heuristics.action: Ask directly how many courses TAs are expected to teach per semester and whether this is standard for the full program duration
heuristics.because: Excessive TA loads signal that the program is using PhD students as cheap labor rather than investing in their research development, structurally delaying graduation

decision_factors.factor: Advisor publication network (insular vs. broadly collaborative)
decision_factors.why_it_matters: An advisor who only publishes with their own students cannot connect you to the broader academic community, limiting your professional network and future collaborations at the moment you need them most — job market
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Search the advisor on Google Scholar; manually check the last 10–15 co-authors and identify what percentage are current or former students vs. peers at other institutions

decision_factors.factor: Documented advisor behavior patterns (broken promises, student departures, disorganization)
decision_factors.why_it_matters: These patterns directly predict PhD completion risk; a disorganized advisor who makes and breaks commitments is a structural blocker to graduation, not a manageable inconvenience
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Ask former students directly about advisor reliability; check attrition rate from the lab; ask the advisor about former students and what they are doing now

decision_factors.factor: Program TA load and structural use of PhD students
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Programs that systematically overload PhD students with teaching are trading student research progress for departmental instructional coverage — this extends time-to-degree and delays publications
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Ask current students how many courses they TA per semester, whether this changes after the first year, and whether RA funding options exist as an alternative

decision_factors.factor: Lab peer culture — genuine vs. trauma-bonded cohesion
decision_factors.why_it_matters: A close-knit student group can reflect healthy mentorship or can be a coping mechanism for surviving a dysfunctional advisor; confusing the two leads to misreading lab culture as a positive signal
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Ask students what they would change about their lab or program; ask whether they have considered switching advisors; observe whether conversations about the PI are enthusiastic or carefully qualified

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Advisors who demand publishable work or formed research ideas within the first weeks of a PhD (especially for students without a prior master's) are signaling unrealistic expectations that will persist and escalate
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Ask the advisor directly what they expect from a student in the first semester; ask current first- and second-year students what their advisor expected of them early on

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Joining a lab with strong peer cohesion as a positive signal
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Tight student bonds may reflect a support network built to survive a dysfunctional advisor, not a sign of healthy lab culture — the cohesion is a coping mechanism, not an indicator of mentorship quality
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Applicants who weigh 'community feel' heavily during visit weekends and interpret student closeness as evidence the lab is a good place to work

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Choosing a program because of one exceptional professor
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: If that professor leaves, loses funding, retires, or proves to be a poor mentor, the student has no viable alternative advisor and may face program exit or an unplanned restart
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: PhD applicants who identify one perfect advisor match and treat that match as sufficient justification to accept an offer, regardless of broader program fit

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Accepting a program with high TA load in exchange for funding
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: The TA commitment consumes the time nominally available for research, extending time-to-degree and delaying publications — the cost is paid in years, not dollars
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Students who calculate funding in terms of stipend amount without accounting for the research-hours cost of fulfilling the TA requirement

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Joining a lab with an advisor who has a large publication record
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: If that publication record is built primarily on co-authoring with advisees rather than peers, the prestige of the record does not translate into a professional network for the student — the advisor's citations don't open doors they haven't opened themselves
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Students who use publication count or h-index as a primary proxy for advisor quality without examining the co-author composition

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Staying with a problematic advisor because the department resources, location, or peer group are strong
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Great facilities and a supportive cohort cannot compensate for an advisor who does not graduate students; the advisor determines whether you finish — everything else is secondary
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Students who rationalize remaining with a documented red-flag advisor because the surrounding environment is appealing

failure_patterns.pattern: Accepting a PhD offer at a high-prestige program despite documented advisor red flags, rationalizing that the department's resources or rankings will compensate
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Prestige bias and sunk-cost thinking during admissions — applicants overweight the brand value of the institution and underweight the operational reality that the advisor, not the university, determines daily PhD life and graduation
failure_patterns.consequence: Students end up in labs with disorganized, unreliable advisors, experience broken promises, watch peers leave the lab, and face delayed or incomplete dissertations — the prestige of the institution provides no protection once enrolled
warning_signs: Multiple former students have left the lab
Advisor is described as disorganized or poor communicator by current students
Advisor makes specific promises during recruitment that feel unusually accommodating

failure_patterns.pattern: Misreading tight peer cohesion in a lab as evidence of a healthy culture
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Halo effect and social proof — a warm, close-knit student group feels like a positive signal, and applicants do not probe whether that closeness is a support structure built around surviving dysfunction
failure_patterns.consequence: Student joins a lab expecting community support only to discover the camaraderie is a coping mechanism; the advisor problems remain and the student must also navigate them
warning_signs: Students speak warmly about each other but carefully or vaguely about the PI
Students mention 'having each other's backs' in contexts that don't quite fit a healthy lab
Questions about the advisor are redirected to talk about the cohort

failure_patterns.pattern: International students accepting first-semester overload (heavy coursework + multiple TA positions) without understanding program norms and then being labeled 'underperforming'
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Power asymmetry and cultural adjustment — international students are less likely to push back on demands, less familiar with what is structurally normal, and more afraid of jeopardizing their visa status or funding
failure_patterns.consequence: Students internalize the 'underperforming' label as personal failure rather than recognizing it as an unreasonable structural expectation; this damages confidence and delays seeking help
warning_signs: Advisor compares the student unfavorably to others in the first semester
Advisor uses language like 'might be dismissed' within the first few months
Student is carrying 9+ credit hours plus two TA positions simultaneously

failure_patterns.pattern: Advisor submitting student work to journals without student consent or adding their name to student publications without contribution
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Power asymmetry — students lack the institutional knowledge or leverage to challenge a supervisor who controls their funding, degree progress, and recommendations
failure_patterns.consequence: Student loses credit for their own work; the advisor's publication record grows at the student's expense; the behavior is protected by the advisor's academic standing
warning_signs: Advisor selects students who are unlikely to challenge them
Advisor restricts students to prescribed topics that align with the advisor's agenda
Advisor's entire publication list consists of co-authorships with advisees

diagnostic_questions.question: What are former students from this lab doing now, and can I contact them directly?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the advisor successfully graduates and places students, and whether alumni are willing to speak candidly — an advisor who stonewalls this question or whose former students are unreachable is a red flag
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Ask former students directly whether the advisor kept commitments, how they handled conflict, and whether they would repeat the experience
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Ask why contacting former students is difficult and look for lab attrition data through other channels

diagnostic_questions.question: How many co-authors on this advisor's recent publications are their own current or former students vs. independent peers?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the advisor collaborates broadly in the field or operates as a closed loop — insularity in publishing predicts a limited professional network for you after graduation
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Assess whether the peer collaborators are in subfields relevant to your interests and could serve as references or collaborators for you
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Ask the advisor directly about collaborations outside the lab and why their publication record is so internally focused

diagnostic_questions.question: How many students have left this lab before completing their PhD in the last five years?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Structural dysfunction — high attrition from a single lab, when not explained by funding changes, is the clearest leading indicator of advisor problems
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Ask the advisor or program coordinator to explain the departures; evasive or blame-shifting answers are themselves a red flag
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Treat as a positive signal but continue checking other dimensions — low attrition in a small lab can also reflect students being afraid to leave

diagnostic_questions.question: What does the advisor expect from a student in the first semester — specifically in terms of research output?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the advisor has realistic expectations calibrated to a student's actual stage of development, or whether they will apply pressure for publishable results before the student has the foundation to produce them
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Ask current first-year students whether the stated expectations match the lived experience
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: A vague or dismissive answer ('just get settled in') should prompt follow-up with current students about whether expectations become clear later and how

diagnostic_questions.question: If the one professor I came here to work with left tomorrow, would I still want to be in this program?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Whether the program has enough depth — in faculty, resources, and fit — to sustain a PhD independently of a single advisor relationship
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Identify the other faculty members and assess whether those relationships are genuine or hypothetical
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: This is a strong signal to reconsider the offer or to conduct a broader faculty search before committing

industry_realities.common_belief: A tight-knit, supportive student community is a reliable indicator of a healthy lab and good advisor
industry_realities.actual_reality: Strong peer bonds in a lab can be a trauma-bonding coping mechanism built specifically because the advisor is dysfunctional — the support is real, but it exists to survive the problem, not because the problem doesn't exist
industry_realities.implication: Applicants should probe why the community is close, not just whether it is close — the same outcome (tight bonds) can have diametrically opposite causes

industry_realities.common_belief: A professor with a large publication record is a strong advisor because they are clearly productive and know how to publish
industry_realities.actual_reality: If that publication record is built almost entirely on co-authoring with current and former advisees, it signals insularity rather than academic standing — the advisor may be extracting productivity from students rather than generating it collaboratively
industry_realities.implication: Always examine the composition of co-authors, not just the count of publications; an h-index built on student labor does not translate into a peer network for you

industry_realities.common_belief: Prestige and resources of a top-ranked program are enough to overcome a problematic advisor
industry_realities.actual_reality: The advisor, not the institution, determines whether a PhD student graduates on time, gets publications, and receives strong recommendations — facilities and rankings are irrelevant if the advisor is the blocker
industry_realities.implication: Documented red flags about an advisor should be treated as disqualifying regardless of institutional prestige; there is no prestige discount on advisor dysfunction

industry_realities.common_belief: First-semester PhD students who cannot produce research ideas quickly are underperforming
industry_realities.actual_reality: First publications typically emerge in years 2–3; expecting formed research ideas within weeks of enrollment (especially without a prior master's) reflects unrealistic advisor expectations, not student failure
industry_realities.implication: Students receiving early 'underperforming' labels should benchmark against program norms by speaking with other students and program coordinators before internalizing the label

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: How to evaluate a potential PhD advisor
junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Check the advisor's h-index, publication count, grant funding, and department ranking — treat these as proxies for advisor quality
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Examine co-author composition on recent publications, ask former students about reliability and promise-keeping, check lab attrition, and look for alignment between what the advisor says during recruitment and what current students report
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Metrics are gameable through exploitative advising practices; the operational quality of the advisor-student relationship is only visible through qualitative investigation

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: How to interpret visit weekend dynamics
junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Treat visit weekend as a chance to be evaluated; focus on impressing faculty and fitting in with students; interpret a warm reception as a good sign
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Treat visit weekend as a two-way evaluation; actively probe current students for qualified enthusiasm, pauses before praise, and what they would change; recognize that candidates who ask hard questions are demonstrating exactly the judgment good programs want
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Applicants who fail to evaluate the program during visit weekend miss the only low-cost opportunity to gather candid information before a five-year commitment

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: How to think about advisor-student fit vs. program prestige
junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Rank programs by prestige and accept the highest-ranked offer; assume the brand will open doors regardless of advisor quality
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Treat advisor quality as the primary variable and program prestige as a secondary tiebreaker; a lower-ranked program with a reliable, well-networked advisor produces better career outcomes than a top program with a dysfunctional one
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: The career leverage that prestige provides depends on completing the degree and receiving strong recommendations — both of which require a functional advisor relationship

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: How to respond to early pressure from a new advisor
junior_vs_senior_signals.naive_pattern: Internalize the advisor's framing ('you might be underperforming') as accurate feedback and increase effort without questioning whether the expectation is reasonable
junior_vs_senior_signals.informed_pattern: Benchmark the expectation against program norms by talking to peers and other faculty; recognize when pressure reflects the advisor's dysfunction rather than the student's performance; seek clarification on expectations in writing
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Internalizing unreasonable expectations as personal failure damages confidence and delays the student from seeking structural remedies (advisor change, program ombudsperson, etc.)

community_misconceptions.misconception: If a program is top-ranked and has great facilities, the advisor's personal issues won't be a dealbreaker — the environment compensates
community_misconceptions.why_believed: Prestige is visible and measurable; advisor dysfunction is invisible until you are inside the lab; applicants overweight what they can see and underweight what they cannot
community_misconceptions.actual_rule: The advisor is the single most important variable in PhD success — they control your funding, publications, recommendations, and ultimately your graduation; no amount of departmental prestige neutralizes a documented dysfunctional advisor
community_misconceptions.real_consequence: Students accept offers at prestigious programs with red-flag advisors, experience broken promises and student departures, and face delayed or failed dissertations while the institution's brand offers no protection

community_misconceptions.misconception: A professor who publishes a lot with their students is a great mentor — they clearly invest in student development
community_misconceptions.why_believed: High co-authorship with students superficially resembles mentorship investment; it is easy to confuse volume of shared publications with quality of the mentoring relationship
community_misconceptions.actual_rule: If the publication record is exclusively with current and former students and not with independent peers, it may indicate the advisor is extracting student labor rather than collaborating broadly — and it signals insularity that limits the student's network
community_misconceptions.real_consequence: Students join labs expecting mentorship and a professional network, only to discover the advisor's collaborations are internally closed and offer no external connections upon graduation

community_misconceptions.misconception: First-semester PhD students who can't generate strong research ideas immediately are falling behind
community_misconceptions.why_believed: Advisors who apply this pressure frame it as a standard, and students — especially international students new to the system — have no calibration benchmark to contradict it
community_misconceptions.actual_rule: First publications in PhD programs typically emerge in years 2–3; expecting formed, actionable research ideas within the first weeks of enrollment is structurally unreasonable, not a legitimate performance standard
community_misconceptions.real_consequence: Students internalize false underperformance labels, lose confidence, and delay seeking structural help — sometimes leaving programs unnecessarily or suffering prolonged distress

real_case_outcomes.situation: Master's student whose advisor neglected paperwork, submitted student work to journals without consent, added their name to student publications, and selected compliant students unlikely to challenge them
real_case_outcomes.decision: Student remained in the program under this advisor; the advisor's extensive publication record (built on student co-authorships) protected their academic position despite the behavior
real_case_outcomes.outcome: The advisor faced no institutional consequences; the student's work was published without their full consent or credit; the advisor's insularity was structurally rewarded
real_case_outcomes.lesson: A large publication record built on student co-authorships can protect an exploitative advisor from accountability — the metric that looks like success is the same mechanism enabling the exploitation

real_case_outcomes.situation: First-semester CS PhD student (no prior master's) assigned 9 credit hours of coursework plus two TA positions; newly-promoted advisor demanded research ideas within weeks and threatened dismissal for 'underperforming'
real_case_outcomes.decision: Student sought community advice rather than immediately accepting the framing
real_case_outcomes.outcome: Community consensus confirmed the expectations were structurally unreasonable; the student was advised to benchmark against program norms and seek clarification rather than internalizing the label
real_case_outcomes.lesson: First-semester underperformance labels applied before normal research ramp-up periods (years 2–3) reflect advisor dysfunction, not student failure — especially for international students carrying teaching loads simultaneously with coursework

real_case_outcomes.situation: STEM PhD applicant choosing between School A (strong advisor, weaker resources, small isolated lab) and School B (documented red-flag advisor — disorganization, broken promises, multiple student departures — but excellent facilities, department, and peer group)
real_case_outcomes.decision: Community strongly advised choosing School A
real_case_outcomes.outcome: Thread reached strong consensus: advisor quality is the determinative variable; School B's resources cannot compensate for an advisor with documented failures of reliability and student retention
real_case_outcomes.lesson: When an advisor has documented red flags (broken promises, student departures, disorganization), those signals predict your PhD experience more accurately than any other program variable — do not trade a functional advisor for prestige or resources

real_case_outcomes.situation: Applicant asked a recent program graduate about their experience during a campus visit
real_case_outcomes.decision: The graduate paused visibly before saying 'yeah...it's a really great program' with little enthusiasm; the applicant noticed and withdrew their application
real_case_outcomes.outcome: Not explicitly stated, but the applicant treated the signal as sufficient to decline
real_case_outcomes.lesson: The quality of enthusiasm from current and recent students during campus visits is a leading indicator — genuine excitement is expressed naturally; performed, qualified, or hesitant praise after a pause reveals what the speaker cannot say directly

psychological_barriers.trigger: Applicant receives an offer from a prestigious program with a known red-flag advisor and asks whether the program's resources and ranking can compensate
psychological_barriers.underlying_state: Prestige anxiety and loss aversion — the applicant fears turning down a top-ranked offer more than they fear the documented advisor problems; the brand feels like a known quantity while the advisor problems feel like a manageable risk
psychological_barriers.how_it_manifests: Applicant lists the program's positive attributes at length and frames advisor red flags as 'concerns' or 'things to watch' rather than disqualifying evidence; seeks permission from the community to accept
psychological_barriers.expert_move: Reframe the question from 'can the program compensate for the advisor?' to 'does this advisor have a track record of graduating students and keeping commitments?' — force the applicant to answer the operational question rather than the prestige question

psychological_barriers.trigger: International student is told by their advisor in the first semester that they may be 'underperforming' and faces comparison to other students
psychological_barriers.underlying_state: Power asymmetry fear and imposter syndrome — international students are acutely aware of their visa dependency on program standing and are less likely to have the cultural calibration to know whether the expectation is reasonable
psychological_barriers.how_it_manifests: Student internalizes the label as personal failure, increases workload unsustainably, avoids seeking help from peers or program administrators, and does not challenge whether the standard is structurally normal
psychological_barriers.expert_move: Immediately provide a benchmark — first publications emerge in years 2–3; first-semester expectations are coursework adjustment, not research output — and direct the student to gather data from peers before accepting the advisor's framing

psychological_barriers.trigger: Applicant visits a PhD program, finds the student cohort warm and tightly bonded, and uses this as a primary positive signal
psychological_barriers.underlying_state: Social proof bias — humans use group cohesion as a heuristic for safety and quality; a close community feels like evidence that the environment is good
psychological_barriers.how_it_manifests: Applicant reports the 'great community' as a key reason to accept without probing whether the closeness is a support structure built around surviving dysfunction
psychological_barriers.expert_move: Ask the applicant to distinguish between: 'students enjoy each other because the environment is healthy' vs. 'students rely on each other because the advisor is dysfunctional' — then suggest specific probe questions to distinguish the two

psychological_barriers.trigger: Applicant is paralyzed choosing between a well-matched lower-ranked program and a higher-ranked program with one exceptional faculty match but no backup options
psychological_barriers.underlying_state: Single-point optimization fallacy combined with FOMO — the exceptional advisor match feels irreplaceable, and the applicant fears they will regret not taking the 'best' option
psychological_barriers.how_it_manifests: Applicant focuses entirely on the one exceptional professor and discounts the structural risk of having no fallback; asks the community to validate the single-professor choice
psychological_barriers.expert_move: Ask the applicant to answer: 'if this professor left the program tomorrow, would you still want to be here?' — this forces them to evaluate the program on its own merits and surfaces the single-point-of-failure risk

reframing_moves.original_framing: Should I choose School B (great resources, great department, great peers) even though the advisor has some concerning issues?
reframing_moves.reframe: The advisor determines whether you graduate — everything else is secondary. The question is not 'is the program good?' but 'does this advisor have a track record of graduating students and keeping commitments?'
reframing_moves.why_it_works: It shifts the decision criterion from additive (sum of positives) to threshold (one variable as a gate) — applicants who think additively will always find enough positives to rationalize a bad advisor; the reframe forces a pass/fail test on the critical variable
reframing_moves.example_language: Great advisor and meh everything else beats out multiple red flags with the advisor. An effective advisor is essential for graduation.

reframing_moves.original_framing: I'm in my first semester and my advisor says I might be underperforming — am I failing?
reframing_moves.reframe: The question is not whether you are meeting your advisor's expectations — the question is whether your advisor's expectations are reasonable for a first-semester student. Benchmark against program norms before accepting the framing.
reframing_moves.why_it_works: It moves agency from the student (am I good enough?) to the structure (is the expectation calibrated correctly?) — this is not a performance question, it is a norms question, and answering it requires data from peers, not harder work
reframing_moves.example_language: First publications typically emerge in years 2–3. The pressure to produce papers during the first semester was universally deemed unreasonable.

reframing_moves.original_framing: The students at this program are so close and supportive — isn't that a great sign?
reframing_moves.reframe: Close student bonds can mean two completely different things: a healthy culture where everyone thrives, or a survival network built because the advisor is dysfunctional. The outcome looks the same from the outside. You need to find out which one it is.
reframing_moves.why_it_works: It introduces the possibility that the same observable signal has opposite causes — this breaks the heuristic that 'community = good' and motivates the applicant to probe rather than conclude
reframing_moves.example_language: Caution: close relationships among students might stem from needing support to survive a dysfunctional lab — that peer support is a coping mechanism, not a sign of healthy culture.

reframing_moves.original_framing: Is this program worth attending? I asked a recent graduate and they said it was great.
reframing_moves.reframe: Don't evaluate the content of what current students say — evaluate how they say it. Genuine enthusiasm is spontaneous. A pause before 'yeah...it's a really great program' is the signal, not the words.
reframing_moves.why_it_works: It shifts attention from semantic content (the words said) to paralinguistic signals (hesitation, tone, delivery) — experienced evaluators know that what people cannot say directly is often more informative than what they do say
reframing_moves.example_language: Genuine excitement (or lack thereof) from current students is telling. A pattern of muted enthusiasm across multiple students is a significant red flag.
